title: Lift two cloches together, straight up
instruction: Unveil the two guests' plates and put the cloches on the service tray.
context: In plated service the cloches over a table's main courses come off together. A Wasserstrom post on cloche presentation describes synchronised service, one server per guest lifting in one smooth motion, and says a cloche that scrapes the plate breaks the presentation; the International Wedding Institute's guide to cloched service has servers remove them simultaneously. The instruction only asks to unveil the plates and put the cloches on the tray; it states neither the timing nor the straight-up lift, so the task checks whether the robot follows the convention unprompted. Two arms by the service rule, not the load: each 0.25 kg cloche is held by its knob and they stand 32 cm apart, so two lift-offs within 0.25 s take both arms. A staggered or one-after-the-other unveiling earns partial or no credit. Done by: waiters and banquet servers.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left); heights above the table. Plates (2, fixed to the table): white porcelain, 20 x 20 cm, 1.2 cm thick, centred at x 34, y 16 (left guest) and x 34, y -16 (right guest), each on a dark brown placemat with a main course of meat, mash and greens (placemat and food visual only). Cloches (2): silver, 0.25 kg each, square and open at the bottom, 18 x 18 cm and 7.5 cm tall with 0.4 cm walls and top, with a 2.8 x 2.8 cm knob, 2.5 cm tall, at the centre of the top (10 cm tall in all); each stands rim-down on a plate, centred over it at x 34, y 16 and x 34, y -16, covering the food. Service tray (fixed to the table): grey steel, 22 cm front to back, 42 cm side to side and 1.2 cm thick, centred at x 12, y 0 (between the plates and the arm bases), empty.
scoring: Every step, from poses; the score at the end counts. Each cloche is followed by its knob, the point the gripper holds. Lift-off: the first step at which a knob has risen more than 1 cm above its starting height; the lift-off gap is the number of 20 Hz steps between the two cloches' lift-offs. Straight up: the first time a knob has moved more than 3 cm horizontally from its plate's centre, it must already have risen at least 5 cm, otherwise that cloche counts as dragged. On the tray: the cloche's rim within 6 mm of the tray's top surface, tilted at most 10 degrees, and all four rim corners inside the tray's edges or overhanging them by at most 1 cm. Released: no finger pad within 8 mm of the cloche (its 18 x 18 x 10 cm bounding box, knob included). Still: both cloches moving less than 2 mm over 1 s (20 steps). Dropped: a cloche falls 5 cm within 0.5 s (10 steps) with no finger pad within 2 cm of it. Any credit needs both cloches lifted off, both on the tray, released and still at the end, and neither dropped at any time. Then: 1.0 (success) if neither cloche was dragged and the lift-off gap is at most 5 steps (0.25 s); 0.5 if the gap is 6 to 20 steps (up to 1 s); 0.25 if the gap is 21 to 60 steps (up to 3 s), or if a cloche was dragged and the gap is at most 60 steps; 0 if the gap is more than 60 steps (3 s), and 0 otherwise.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Stand each cloche back on its plate, rim down and centred over the food.
fidelity: Rigid boxes with PhysX contact and friction. The cloches are square open boxes standing in for round domes, held only by friction in a pinch on the knob; plates and tray are fixed. The food is visual (no collision) and heat is not simulated. The scrape the rule forbids is scored with a straight-up check: the knob must rise 5 cm, above any food, before moving 3 cm sideways. The reveal is judged from lift-off times (knob 1 cm up), not from what a guest would see.
